title: Rectified Language Flow

paper.title: Rectified Language Flow
paper.abstract:
Abstract Continuous-state flow and diffusion models offer a promising approach to fast, parallel language generation, but matching the generation quality of autoregressive models remains challenging. We present Rectified Language Flow (ReLF), a language model that generates text by transporting noise to token embeddings using rectified flow. ReLF combines several complementary design choices: fixed token embeddings constructed with Hellinger–SVD, self-conditioning guidance trained with cross-entropy, and regularized reflow for few-step generation. We further introduce singular logits, which combine an analytically computed term that drives commitment to a valid token embedding as noise vanishes with a bounded neural residual that learns contextual token preferences. With 64 function evaluations on OpenWebText, ReLF achieves lower generative perplexity than autoregressive baselines at matched diversity across all three model sizes tested, while also outperforming prior continuous flow methods in this setting.
After two reflow rounds, ReLF still outperforms autoregressive baselines with 16 function evaluations while generating 1,024-token sequences 15–19 × \times faster at batch size 1.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Parallel text generation can reduce the sequential cost of autoregressive (AR) decoding. Flow and diffusion models take two approaches: discrete-state models update token identities, whereas continuous-state models evolve real-valued representations decoded into tokens. Discrete approaches have attracted substantial attention through large-scale diffusion language modeling [ 53 , 46 , 60 ] . Building on early continuous text diffusion [ 36 , 23 ] , continuous-state approaches are also gaining momentum, with recent developments in embedding-space modeling and few-step generation [ 34 , 27 ] . Continuous formulations are attractive for two reasons. First, they are flexible: all positions evolve jointly before committing to tokens, so a model transforming noise across the whole sequence can, in principle, capture inter-token dependencies in a single evaluation, the basis for one-step generation [ 34 ] . Second, they inherit image, audio, and video generation tools, namely ODE/SDE samplers, guidance, and trajectory straightening, for controlling generation and accelerating sampling [ 40 , 39 ] . However, turning these advantages into effective language models raises three design challenges: learning continuous dynamics from categorical supervision; reliably recovering tokens at the flow’s end; and designing token embeddings whose geometry supports corruption and denoising. Prior work explored auxiliary objectives [ 36 , 23 ] , encoder–decoder networks [ 42 ] , and vocabulary-sized simplex representations [ 25 , 34 ] . We seek a simple continuous-flow formulation that addresses them while generating high-quality, diverse text with few function evaluations.

sections.heading: Results.
sections.text: We present Re ctified L anguage F low (ReLF), a rectified-flow language model that generates token sequences along continuous embedding trajectories from noise. ReLF predicts a token posterior at each position and is trained only with cross-entropy. The velocity field is computed from the posterior-weighted mean of the token embeddings. Our OpenWebText experiments show: • Generation quality at 64 function evaluations. ReLF outperforms same-size AR baselines and Embedded Language Flows (ELF) [ 27 ] across all evaluated model sizes. ReLF-Small achieves a generative perplexity of 24.1 24.1 at an entropy of 5.45 5.45 nats, compared with 27.7 27.7 at 5.43 5.43 for AR-Small. ReLF-Large reaches 17.3 17.3 at 5.51 5.51 , matching the generative perplexity of real OpenWebText text ( 17.3 17.3 at 5.49 5.49 ). • Faster generation through reflow. We further apply reflow [ 40 ] to reduce the number of function evaluations. After two rounds, ReLF still outperforms same-size AR models with just 16 function evaluations. It then generates 1,024-token sequences 15–19 × \times faster than these AR baselines at batch size 1 (Figure 1 (b)). • Generation quality at 8 function evaluations. With only 8 function evaluations, ReLF-Medium achieves a generative perplexity of 42.7 42.7 , compared with 66.4 66.4 for ELF+PD, a progressively distilled ELF model, both at entropy 5.42 5.42 .

sections.heading: Methods.
sections.text: ReLF learns continuous dynamics from categorical supervision by training token posteriors with cross-entropy (Section 2 ). Four components then address reliable token recovery, embedding geometry, and high-quality generation with few function evaluations: • Singular logits. As noise vanishes, token posteriors approach point masses, requiring unbounded logit differences. Our singular logits capture this divergence analytically through a reference posterior, so the network learns only a bounded residual of contextual token preferences. This guarantees that the modeled posterior converges to a one-hot distribution and the trajectory to a token embedding (Section 3.1 ). • Embedding geometry for language flows. Token embeddings define the geometry of corruption and denoising. Our fixed, frequency-weighted Hellinger–SVD embeddings place tokens with similar contexts nearby. Their dimension is a free hyperparameter, which we find important for generation quality (Section 3.2 ). • Logit-space self-conditioning guidance. Self-conditioning guidance extrapolates between predictions with and without the previous clean estimate, which prior work does in continuous state space [ 9 , 27 ] . We instead extrapolate in logit space, so the guided prediction remains a token distribution, learnable through cross-entropy alone with one function evaluation per step (Section 3.3 ). • Regularized reflow. Regularized reflow retrains the model on its own noise–token couplings and interpolates its weights back toward the base model, straightening the flow for few-step generation while controlling drift (Section 3.4 ).

sections.heading: 3 Commitment, Geometry, Guidance, and Straightening
sections.text: Section 2 fixes the training objective and sampler but leaves open how tokens commit as noise vanishes and in which embedding space the flow evolves. This section addresses both: Section 3.1 introduces singular logits, which guarantee convergence to token embeddings, and Section 3.2 constructs compact, context-informed flow embeddings. We further adapt two widely used flow techniques: Section 3.3 moves self-conditioning guidance to logit space, where it can be trained with CE, and Section 3.4 stabilizes reflow for few-step generation.

sections.heading: Motivation.
sections.text: As noise vanishes, the posterior converges to a one-hot distribution. Under a fixed-temperature softmax, this requires diverging logit differences, which a network with bounded inputs and parameters cannot represent. The predicted posterior thus keeps probability on competing tokens even at the endpoint. Since the trajectory converges to the clean-state estimate X ^ 1 \widehat{X}_{1} , it ends at a mixture of token embeddings rather than at a single token embedding (Figure 3 (a,c)). Prior continuous models instead decode final states by rounding or a separate decoder [ 36 , 27 ] . We observe that the exact posterior itself points to a solution: its logits decompose into a singular component that diverges as noise vanishes and a bounded component carrying contextual token preferences. The singular component has a closed form for a simple reference distribution r 1 r_{1} , leaving the network to learn a residual that is guaranteed to stay finite. sections.heading: 3.2 Construction of Flow Embeddings
sections.text: The embedding matrix E E determines which tokens remain ambiguous under noise. Any embedding with distinct rows recovers the data distribution under exact posteriors and integration, but its geometry controls how difficult these posteriors are to approximate. Nearby embeddings should represent tokens with similar contexts, allowing noisy states to preserve information about neighboring positions before token commitment.

sections.heading: Embedding Dimension.
sections.text: In prior continuous models, the flow dimension is tied to another component: to the vocabulary size in the one-hot and simplex states of FMLM [ 34 ] and SSD-LM [ 25 ] , to the pretrained T5 encoder in ELF [ 27 ] , and to the model width in LangFlow [ 10 ] . In ReLF, the network projects each d d -dimensional state to its hidden width and predicts V V token logits, so d d is decoupled from all three and becomes a free hyperparameter. We use d = 32 d=32 for all model sizes, consistent with compact representations in image diffusion [ 74 , 35 ] ; Section 4.3 compares dimensions 16 to 256.

sections.heading: Dataset and Evaluation.
sections.text: We evaluate unconditional text generation on OpenWebText (OWT) [ 20 ] , following the benchmark used in prior diffusion and flow language models [ 41 , 53 , 34 , 27 ] . We tokenize the corpus with the GPT-2 tokenizer [ 51 ] and pack sequences to length L = 1024 L=1024 . For each ReLF and AR sampling configuration, we generate 1,024 sequences (ELF results use 1,000) and report generative perplexity (Gen. PPL) under GPT-2 Large and sample diversity as the mean per-sequence unigram entropy in nats. We evaluate the quality–diversity trade-off by sweeping the guidance strength.

sections.heading: Model.
sections.text: Our default model is ReLF-Small, a bidirectional diffusion Transformer [ 48 ] with 138M trainable parameters, 12 layers, hidden width 768, and 12 attention heads. We use the fixed 32-dimensional Hellinger–SVD token embeddings constructed in Section 3.2 . At each position, the noisy embedding is concatenated with a self-conditioning estimate of the clean embedding and projected to the Transformer width. The network predicts residual logits, which are added to the analytic singular logits with a unigram reference distribution. Appendix B gives the configurations of all sizes.

sections.heading: Training and Inference.
sections.text: We train ReLF-Small, ReLF-Medium, and ReLF-Large for 80,000 steps each, with a global batch of 1,024 × 1,024 1{,}024\times 1{,}024 tokens (1,024 sequences of length 1,024), minimizing the CE loss in Eq. ( 3 ). We use Muon [ 30 , 7 , 8 ] for hidden matrices and AdamW for the input and output projections, normalization gains, and biases, with a base learning rate of 3 × 10 − 4 3\times 10^{-4} , 2,500 warmup steps, and a constant learning rate thereafter. Training uses standard Gaussian corruption, an embedding-dependent interpolation-time distribution, and self-conditioning with probability 0.5 0.5 . For distilled self-conditioning guidance, each sequence also draws a scale ω \omega log-uniform on [ 1.5 , 6 ] [1.5,6] , as in ELF [ 27 ] . We evaluate exponential-moving-average (EMA) checkpoints with decay 0.9999 0.9999 . We report sampling cost in number of function evaluations (NFE) and wall-clock time; by default, we use the SDE sampler with 64 NFE. At sampling time, we sweep ω \omega ; because ω \omega is a network input, each guided step costs a single forward pass.

sections.heading: 4.2 Unconditional Generation on OpenWebText
sections.text: Figure 1 (a) compares the quality–diversity trade-offs of ReLF, ELF [ 27 ] , and autoregressive (AR) baselines trained on the same data and swept over sampling temperature. Each method has three sizes, Small, Medium, and Large, corresponding to the B, M, and L configurations of Hu et al. [27] (Table 2 ). With 64 NFE, ReLF outperforms both ELF and the AR baseline at every model size across the trade-off. At matched entropy, ReLF-Small, ReLF-Medium, and ReLF-Large reach Gen. PPL 24.1 24.1 , 18.6 18.6 , and 17.3 17.3 , compared with 27.7 27.7 , 22.3 22.3 , and 20.2 20.2 for AR-Small, AR-Medium, and AR-Large. Appendix B.6 gives the evaluation details and the full Pareto frontiers. Observation 1. To the best of our knowledge, ReLF is the first continuous flow language model to achieve lower generative perplexity than autoregressive baselines of the same size on OpenWebText at matched entropy. ReLF-Large is close to real OpenWebText on the two reported metrics. It reaches Gen. PPL 17.3 17.3 at entropy 5.51 5.51 , matching the Gen. PPL of real OpenWebText text ( 17.3 17.3 at 5.49 5.49 ). Unlike the Small and Medium models and despite the identical training pipeline, ReLF-Large no longer trades Gen. PPL against entropy effectively under guidance: across all guidance scales, both metrics stay nearly constant, with Gen. PPL between 17.3 17.3 and 18.0 18.0 (Table 5 ), so only two of its eight settings are non-dominated and appear in Figure 1 (a). This does not mean that its samples fully match real text; the remaining differences in quality and diversity are small, semantic, and beyond what Gen. PPL and unigram entropy resolve (see the samples in Appendix C ). Unconditional OpenWebText generation thus calls for richer benchmarks and metrics.

sections.heading: Few-Step Generation.
sections.text: Figure 5 shows how regularized reflow (Section 3.4 ) improves few-step generation. Figure 10 in Appendix B.7 gives the complementary comparison across rounds at fixed NFE, with round 0 denoting the base model. Across rounds, Gen. PPL decreases at 8, 16, and 32 NFE for every model size while unigram entropy remains similar. Most of the gain arrives within two rounds: at 8 NFE, the first round lowers Gen. PPL by 29–36% (e.g., from 62.5 62.5 to 44.5 44.5 for Large), and the second by a further 8–12%. After two rounds, 16 NFE yields lower Gen. PPL than the base model at 32 NFE for every model size (Figure 7 in Appendix B.5 ). At matched entropy, the two-round models also attain lower Gen. PPL than ELF+PD at every NFE from 8 to 32, and than AR-Small (1,023 NFE) from 16 NFE onward (Table 6 ). Figure 5: Few-step generation across reflow rounds. Gen. PPL (top) and entropy (bottom) versus NFE for Small, Medium, and Large ReLF models after zero to three reflow rounds. At 8 NFE, two reflow rounds reduce Gen. PPL by 40 % 40\% , 41 % 41\% , and 35 % 35\% for Small, Medium, and Large, respectively, relative to the model before reflow. After two rounds, ReLF-Small outperforms ELF+PD [ 27 ] from 8 NFE, and all three sizes match or outperform their AR references from 16 NFE. Dotted lines denote same-size AR models; long-dashed lines denote real OpenWebText. Arrows at 4 NFE mark entropies of the model before reflow that fall below the plotted range.

sections.heading: Wall-Clock Efficiency.
sections.text: Figure 1 (b) compares ReLF-Small, ReLF-Medium, and ReLF-Large (138M, 421M, and 784M parameters) with same-size AR models. Because two reflow rounds suffice for each to reach lower Gen. PPL than its AR counterpart at similar unigram entropy with 16 NFE, we evaluate ReLF at this budget. We time 1,024-token generation on one GPU, with KV caching for AR and CUDA graphs for both methods, defining speedup as AR time divided by ReLF time. We compare a latency-bound regime, measuring latency at batch size 1, with a compute-bound regime, measuring throughput at batch size 64. At batch size 1, the speedups for Small, Medium, and Large are 15.3 × 15.3\times , 17.7 × 17.7\times , and 18.9 × 18.9\times ; at batch size 64, they are 1.7 × 1.7\times , 2.6 × 2.6\times , and 1.8 × 1.8\times . Figure 11 in Appendix B.7 reports latency and throughput across batch sizes. Observation 2. Two rounds of regularized reflow reduce Gen. PPL at 8 NFE by 35–41% while unigram entropy remains similar, and 16 NFE then yields lower Gen. PPL than the base model at 32 NFE. At 16 NFE, ReLF attains lower Gen. PPL than same-size AR models at similar entropy while generating 1,024-token sequences more than 15 × 15\times faster at batch size 1.

sections.heading: Singular Logits.
sections.text: Singular logits improve the quality–diversity trade-off (Figure 6 (a)). Without guidance, the model with singular logits reaches Gen. PPL 57.2 57.2 at entropy 5.48 5.48 , versus 64.2 64.2 at 5.48 5.48 for the model without singular logits, and the curve with singular logits lies below the curve without them across their shared entropy range. The gap widens under strong guidance: from α = 0.5 \alpha=0.5 to 0.7 0.7 , Gen. PPL falls from 29.3 29.3 to 24.0 24.0 with singular logits but only from 37.2 37.2 to 36.3 36.3 without them.

sections.heading: Embedding Matrix.
sections.text: Hellinger–SVD outperforms random Gaussian and one-hot embeddings, all with singular logits (Figure 6 (b)). With SDE sampling at α = 0.2 \alpha=0.2 , Hellinger–SVD reaches Gen. PPL 42.1 42.1 at entropy 5.37 5.37 , compared with 83.6 83.6 at 5.34 5.34 for a 32-dimensional random Gaussian embedding. With Euler sampling, Hellinger–SVD attains lower Gen. PPL and higher entropy than the one-hot embedding at every guidance strength, even though the one-hot model has about 215M parameters versus 138M for the Hellinger–SVD model.

sections.heading: Training Objective.
sections.text: Training with CE yields a better quality–diversity trade-off than training with MSE (Figure 6 (c)). The MSE variant regresses the velocity 𝒗 θ = 1 1 − t ​ ( X ^ 1 − X t ) {\bm{v}}_{\theta}=\tfrac{1}{1-t}(\widehat{X}_{1}-X_{t}) onto X 1 − X 0 X_{1}-X_{0} , as in ELF [ 27 ] , and applies the distilled-guidance shift to this velocity target rather than to the logits. The two models differ only in the training loss. At matched entropy, CE attains lower Gen. PPL: 24.1 24.1 at entropy 5.45 5.45 ( ω = 1.7 \omega=1.7 ) versus 25.6 25.6 at 5.45 5.45 for MSE ( ω = 2.8 \omega=2.8 ).

sections.heading: Flow Embedding Dimension.
sections.text: The default 32-dimensional flow embedding space gives the best quality–diversity trade-off (Figure 6 (d)). We vary d ∈ { 16 , 32 , 64 , 128 , 256 } d\in\{16,32,64,128,256\} , retaining the leading d d Hellinger–SVD directions (Section 3.2 ) and normalizing the unigram-weighted mean squared norm to d d ; only the input projection depends on d d . Larger dimensions shift the curve toward higher entropy and need much stronger guidance to lower Gen. PPL. Even at ω = 2.8 \omega=2.8 and 2.6 2.6 , d = 128 d=128 and d = 256 d=256 remain at Gen. PPL 27.3 27.3 and 42.1 42.1 (entropies 5.42 5.42 and 5.58 5.58 ). d = 64 d=64 needs ω = 2.4 \omega=2.4 to reach 23.7 23.7 at 5.48 5.48 , whereas d = 32 d=32 reaches 23.6 23.6 at 5.45 5.45 with ω = 1.8 \omega=1.8 . Reducing the dimension to d = 16 d=16 also hurts: its curve lies above that of d = 32 d=32 . Table 3 in Appendix B.5 lists the plotted values. Observation 3. Singular logits, Hellinger–SVD embeddings, and CE training each lower Gen. PPL at matched entropy, and a 32-dimensional flow space gives the best quality–diversity trade-off.

sections.heading: Sampling Budget.
sections.text: Figure 6 (e) varies only the number of steps within a fixed grid family (Appendix B.4 ) at the default guidance scale ω = 1.7 \omega=1.7 . Gen. PPL drops sharply as NFE grows to the default 64 and decreases further at 256 NFE, with lower entropy.

sections.heading: Guidance and Model Size.
sections.text: Figure 6 (f) compares the guidance response across model sizes. Larger models lose less entropy as guidance increases; ReLF-Large maintains nearly constant Gen. PPL and entropy across the sweep. Figure 8 in Appendix B.7 compares these responses with the AR and ELF quality–diversity trade-offs.

sections.heading: Discrete-State Models.
sections.text: Discrete-state models generate sequences by updating categorical variables, often at multiple positions per step. Following masked-token pretraining [ 15 ] and iterative refinement [ 19 ] , D3PM formalized structured categorical corruption [ 2 ] , while continuous-time Markov formulations established corresponding denoising dynamics [ 5 ] . Subsequent work develops discrete score estimation, simplified masked-denoising objectives, and time-independent parameterizations [ 41 , 53 , 59 , 47 ] , alongside more general corruption kernels and probability paths [ 18 , 57 , 64 ] . The LLaDA family [ 46 , 75 , 4 ] advances masked diffusion through scaling and preference optimization, alongside work on language and code generation [ 69 , 22 , 60 ] and uniform-state diffusion [ 54 , 55 , 71 ] . Sampling research develops blockwise decoding [ 1 ] , remasking [ 65 ] , and adaptive token ordering and parallel updates [ 32 , 67 , 3 ] . Reinforcement learning supports reasoning [ 73 ] , while masked generation extends to images and multimodal modeling [ 6 , 68 ] . These models retain categorical states even when time is continuous.

sections.heading: Continuous-State Models.
sections.text: Continuous-state models generate categorical sequences through real-valued representations, with early examples including Argmax Flows [ 26 ] . Diffusion-LM [ 36 ] used token-embedding diffusion for controllable text generation, while Analog Bits [ 9 ] introduced self-conditioning for diffusion over continuous relaxations of binary encodings. Subsequent embedding-space models incorporate self-conditioning [ 61 ] , continuous-time formulations [ 16 ] , conditional generation and pretraining [ 21 , 38 , 70 ] , and likelihood-based training [ 23 ] . Alternative representations include vocabulary-sized logit/simplex states [ 25 , 31 , 63 ] and statistical-manifold constructions [ 29 , 12 , 11 ] . Latent diffusion denoises encoded text representations with a separate decoder [ 42 , 72 , 56 , 44 , 58 ] , with recent work jointly learning the latent space and generative dynamics [ 45 , 24 ] . Rectified flow has also been applied to conditional text generation [ 28 ] , while continuous flow-map language models pursue few-step decoding through distillation [ 34 , 52 , 49 ] . LangFlow [ 10 ] uses a Bregman formulation to train embedding-space flows with cross-entropy, whereas ELF [ 27 ] performs rectified flow in pretrained contextual embeddings and applies token-level supervision only at final decoding. Within this family, ReLF combines analytic singular logits for endpoint commitment with a compact, context-informed flow embedding space under a single cross-entropy objective, and reaches few-step generation through regularized reflow rather than distillation.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We introduced ReLF, a continuous rectified-flow language model trained with a cross-entropy loss. Its singular logits capture the divergent part of the token posteriors analytically, so trajectories converge to token embeddings, while the bounded learned residual decides which tokens are generated. Fixed Hellinger–SVD embeddings place tokens with similar contexts nearby, self-conditioning guidance in logit space is distilled through the same CE objective, and regularized reflow straightens the flow for few-step generation. On OpenWebText at 64 NFE, ReLF outperforms ELF and autoregressive baselines of the same size, and ReLF-Large matches real text in Gen. PPL at similar entropy. After two reflow rounds, ReLF keeps its advantage over same-size autoregressive models at 16 NFE while generating 15–19 × \times faster at batch size 1. These results show that continuous flows can match autoregressive quality while offering fast, parallel generation.

sections.heading: Corpus Split and Sequence Packing.
sections.text: We use the OpenWebText training split, reserving the last 100,000 documents for validation and training on the rest. Each document is tokenized with the GPT-2 tokenizer and followed by an EOS token, and documents are concatenated within each preprocessing batch. We divide the stream into blocks of 1,022 tokens, discard the incomplete remainder, and add BOS and EOS to obtain sequences of length 1,024; GPT-2 uses the same token ID for both. Token distributions are defined over the 50,257-token GPT-2 vocabulary, excluding padding entries.

sections.heading: Offline Statistics and Smoothing Selection.
sections.text: Embedding construction uses packed training windows sampled from contiguous chunks spread across the corpus, with a quarter of the chunks held out from count estimation for offline embedding evaluation. Adjacent-token pairs are counted within packed windows, including special tokens. The smoothing strength of the two-sided context distribution Q a ​ ( c ) Q_{a}(c) of Appendix A.4 is selected by held-out log loss on validation windows, giving τ = 2000 \tau=2000 .

Model Architecture.
sections.text: We parameterize the neural residual in ReLF with a bidirectional diffusion Transformer on sequences of 1,024 tokens, using the fixed 32-dimensional embeddings of Table 1 . At each position, we concatenate the noisy embedding with a 32-dimensional self-conditioning estimate of the clean embedding and project the result to the Transformer width. Each block combines multi-head self-attention with rotary positional embeddings (RoPE) [ 62 ] , query–key RMS normalization, a sigmoid gate on the attention output [ 50 ] , and a SwiGLU feed-forward network. Both sublayers use RMS normalization with time-dependent affine modulation and residual gates, driven by a sinusoidal time embedding followed by a two-layer MLP, and dropout 0.1 0.1 on the residual branches. A final time-modulated RMS normalization and linear projection produce vocabulary logits, to which we add the analytic singular logits with the unigram reference distribution, except in the ablation that removes this term. Table 2 summarizes the configurations. Small, Medium, and Large match the hidden widths and depths of ELF-B, ELF-M, and ELF-L [ 27 ] , which we accordingly call ELF-Small, ELF-Medium, and ELF-Large. We implement attention with FlashAttention [ 13 , 14 ] ; for compatibility with its backward kernels, Medium and Large use 11 and 20 heads instead of ELF’s 16, while Small keeps ELF’s 12. sections.heading: Model Training.
sections.text: All reported models use a global batch of 1,024 sequences with the preprocessing of Appendix B.1 . We minimize token-averaged cross-entropy, drawing interpolation times by stratified inverse-CDF sampling from the embedding’s precomputed training-time distribution on [ 0 , t end ] [0,t_{\mathrm{end}}] , with no time-dependent loss weight. For self-conditioning, a forward pass without gradient tracking estimates the clean embedding at the same noisy input and time; independently for each sequence, we keep this estimate with probability 0.5 0.5 and otherwise replace it with zero. We optimize hidden, time-embedding, and modulation matrices with Muon (Nesterov momentum 0.95 0.95 , weight decay 0.02 0.02 ), and the input and output projections, normalization gains, and biases with AdamW ( β 1 = 0.9 \beta_{1}=0.9 , β 2 = 0.99 \beta_{2}=0.99 , no weight decay). Both use a base learning rate of 3 × 10 − 4 3\times 10^{-4} with 2,500 linear warmup steps followed by a constant schedule; Muon matches its update RMS to AdamW. Training uses bfloat16 mixed precision, gradient clipping at norm 1.0 1.0 , and an EMA with decay 0.9999 0.9999 for evaluation.

sections.heading: Reflow Training.
sections.text: Couplings are generated from the EMA weights of θ k \theta_{k} with 256-NFE Euler sampling, at guidance scale ω = 1.3 \omega=1.3 in the first round and without guidance ( ω = 1 \omega=1 ) in the second, giving about 0.5M noise–sequence couplings per round. Each round fine-tunes for 4,000 steps with batch size 512 and learning rate 10 − 4 10^{-4} . Eq. ( 11 ) uses λ = 0.7 \lambda=0.7 in the first round and λ = 0.55 \lambda=0.55 in the second.

sections.heading: Compute Accounting.
sections.text: A training run of the default Small configuration takes approximately 300 NVIDIA GH200 GPU-hours.

sections.heading: Numerical Precision.
sections.text: The Transformer residual stream and vocabulary projection run in bfloat16, while the flow state, analytic singular logits, and posterior embedding expectations stay in FP32. Network logits are promoted to FP32 before the analytic term is added, and the softmax and probability-weighted embedding sum are computed in FP32. This limits rounding of token-logit differences as the singular term grows near the endpoint and avoids storing small integration increments in bfloat16. Sampling updates, the self-conditioning carry, and the momentum-guidance velocity average also remain in FP32. Grid nodes and interval coefficients are computed in FP64.

sections.heading: Memory-Efficient Vocabulary Operations.
sections.text: We limit the memory of vocabulary-sized tensors by processing token positions in chunks. During training, each chunk of hidden features is projected to vocabulary logits, augmented with the analytic term, and passed to a fused cross-entropy kernel. A custom autograd operation computes each chunk’s hidden-feature and output-head gradients immediately and saves them for the outer backward pass, so training never materializes the full logit tensor. The self-conditioning pass likewise computes embedding expectations chunk by chunk. During sampling, the network produces the full bfloat16 logit tensor, but singular-logit addition, softmax, and the embedding expectation are performed in FP32 chunks, and final decoding applies a chunkwise argmax.

sections.heading: Scale Conditioning.
sections.text: To obtain guided predictions from a single evaluation, the network receives ω \omega as an input. For each training sequence, we draw ω \omega log-uniformly on [ 1.5 , 6 ] [1.5,6] , the same distribution as in ELF. The scale is encoded by a sinusoidal embedding and a two-layer MLP, mirroring the time embedding, and added to the time embedding that drives the adaptive normalization and residual gates. The final MLP layer is zero-initialized, so the network initially ignores ω \omega .

sections.text: Let l ∗ l^{*} denote the log-posterior that CE fits for the self-conditioned input without the shift. For k = 1 k=1 , CE drives l θ ​ ( ⋅ , 𝑪 , ω ) − Δ l_{\theta}(\cdot;{\bm{C}},\omega)-\Delta toward l ∗ l^{*} up to an additive constant. At a stationary point where the no-gradient warm pass agrees with the gradient-carrying pass, l c = l θ ​ ( ⋅ , 𝑪 , ω ) l^{\mathrm{c}}=l_{\theta}(\cdot;{\bm{C}},\omega) , so 1 ω ​ l θ ​ ( ⋅ , 𝑪 , ω ) + ( 1 − 1 ω ) ​ l u = l ∗ ⟹ l θ ​ ( ⋅ , 𝑪 , ω ) = l u + ω ⁡ ( l ∗ − l u ) , \tfrac{1}{\omega}\,l_{\theta}(\cdot;{\bm{C}},\omega)+\bigl(1-\tfrac{1}{\omega}\bigr)\,l^{\mathrm{u}}=l^{*}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad l_{\theta}(\cdot;{\bm{C}},\omega)=l^{\mathrm{u}}+\omega\bigl(l^{*}-l^{\mathrm{u}}\bigr), again up to an additive constant. sections.heading: Relation to ELF.
sections.text: ELF [ 27 ] uses the same construction, conditioning the network on a per-example guidance scale and building the target from its own stop-gradient cold and warm predictions, but applies the shift to an MSE velocity target, 𝒗 + ( 1 − 1 / ω ) ​ sg ⁡ [ 𝒗 θ ​ ( 𝑪 ) − 𝒗 θ ​ ( 𝟎 ) ] {\bm{v}}+(1-1/\omega)\,\operatorname{sg}[{\bm{v}}_{\theta}({\bm{C}})-{\bm{v}}_{\theta}(\mathbf{0})] . Its guidance therefore extrapolates the clean-embedding estimate linearly, whereas ours extrapolates the token logits as in Eq. ( 16 ) and takes the clean estimate as the mean embedding under the guided posterior p g p^{\mathrm{g}} ; the two generally differ. ELF also trains a separate unguided CE decoding branch, while our guidance enters the only training objective.

sections.heading: Training and Inference.
sections.text: Models with distilled self-conditioning guidance are trained from scratch with the recipe of Appendix B.2 . Relative to plain self-conditioning, each training step needs one additional forward pass without gradient tracking, since the cold pass also supplies the self-conditioning estimate. At inference, we feed a fixed ω \omega to every evaluation, including the first and the final decoding evaluation, use one function evaluation per step, and carry the guided clean estimate as the self-conditioning input.

sections.heading: Evaluation Protocol.
sections.text: For each plotted point, we generate 1,024 unconditional sequences of 1,024 tokens from the EMA parameters of the final checkpoint. We report generative perplexity and mean per-sequence unigram entropy. For generative perplexity, we decode the samples to text, retokenize them with the GPT-2 Large evaluator’s tokenizer, truncate to at most 1,024 tokens, and exponentiate the mean next-token negative log-likelihood over all scored tokens, which include non-EOS targets and the first EOS in each sequence. For diversity, we compute the unigram entropy of each generated sequence in nats and average across samples.

sections.heading: Inference Settings.
sections.text: We sample with a nonuniform time grid and a time-dependent SDE noise level, tuned once on the default Small model at 64 NFE and shared across model sizes; Euler sampling uses the same grid. In the sampling-budget ablation, only the number of grid points changes. Self-conditioning starts from zero and carries the previous clean estimate between steps, so each step requires one function evaluation, and the last evaluation decodes each position by argmax. Momentum guidance [ 37 ] extrapolates the current velocity away from an exponential moving average of previous velocities; we fix its base decay to β = 0.8 \beta=0.8 and sweep the guidance strength α ∈ { 0 , 0.1 , 0.2 , 0.3 , 0.5 , 0.7 } \alpha\in\{0,0.1,0.2,0.3,0.5,0.7\} , where α = 0 \alpha=0 is the unguided baseline.

We present Rectified Language Flow (ReLF), a language model that generates text by transporting noise to token embeddings using rectified flow. ReLF combines several complementary design choices: fixed token embeddings constructed with Hellinger–SVD, self-conditioning guidance trained with cross-entropy, and regularized reflow for few-step generation. We further introduce singular logits, which combine an analytically computed term that drives commitment to a valid token embedding as noise vanishes with a bounded neural residual that learns contextual token preferences. With 64 function evaluations on OpenWebText, ReLF achieves lower generative perplexity than autoregressive baselines at matched diversity across all three model sizes tested, while also outperforming prior continuous flow methods in this setting. After two reflow rounds, ReLF still outperforms autoregressive baselines with 16 function evaluations while generating 1,024-token sequences 15–19 × \times faster at batch size 1. With 16 NFE after two reflow rounds, ReLF achieves lower Generative PPL than these AR models at similar entropy. 1 Introduction Parallel text generation can reduce the sequential cost of autoregressive (AR) decoding. Flow and diffusion models take two approaches: discrete-state models update token identities, whereas continuous-state models evolve real-valued representations decoded into tokens. Discrete approaches have attracted substantial attention through large-scale diffusion language modeling [ 53 , 46 , 60 ] . Building on early continuous text diffusion [ 36 , 23 ] , continuous-state approaches are also gaining momentum, with recent developments in embedding-space modeling and few-step generation [ 34 , 27 ] . Continuous formulations are attractive for two reasons. First, they are flexible: all positions evolve jointly before committing to tokens, so a model transforming noise across the whole sequence can, in principle, capture inter-token dependencies in a single evaluation, the basis for one-step generation [ 34 ] . Second, they inherit image, audio, and video generation tools, namely ODE/SDE samplers, guidance, and trajectory straightening, for controlling generation and accelerating sampling [ 40 , 39 ] . However, turning these advantages into effective language models raises three design challenges: learning continuous dynamics from categorical supervision; reliably recovering tokens at the flow’s end; and designing token embeddings whose geometry supports corruption and denoising. Prior work explored auxiliary objectives [ 36 , 23 ] , encoder–decoder networks [ 42 ] , and vocabulary-sized simplex representations [ 25 , 34 ] . We seek a simple continuous-flow formulation that addresses them while generating high-quality, diverse text with few function evaluations. Results. We present Re ctified L anguage F low (ReLF), a rectified-flow language model that generates token sequences along continuous embedding trajectories from noise. ReLF predicts a token posterior at each position and is trained only with cross-entropy. The velocity field is computed from the posterior-weighted mean of the token embeddings. Our OpenWebText experiments show: • Generation quality at 64 function evaluations. ReLF outperforms same-size AR baselines and Embedded Language Flows (ELF) [ 27 ] across all evaluated model sizes. ReLF-Small achieves a generative perplexity of 24.1 24.1 at an entropy of 5.45 5.45 nats, compared with 27.7 27.7 at 5.43 5.43 for AR-Small. ReLF-Large reaches 17.3 17.3 at 5.51 5.51 , matching the generative perplexity of real OpenWebText text ( 17.3 17.3 at 5.49 5.49 ). • Faster generation through reflow. We further apply reflow [ 40 ] to reduce the number of function evaluations. After two rounds, ReLF still outperforms same-size AR models with just 16 function evaluations. It then generates 1,024-token sequences 15–19 × \times faster than these AR baselines at batch size 1 (Figure 1 (b)). • Generation quality at 8 function evaluations. With only 8 function evaluations, ReLF-Medium achieves a generative perplexity of 42.7 42.7 , compared with 66.4 66.4 for ELF+PD, a progressively distilled ELF model, both at entropy 5.42 5.42 . Methods. ReLF learns continuous dynamics from categorical supervision by training token posteriors with cross-entropy (Section 2 ). Four components then address reliable token recovery, embedding geometry, and high-quality generation with few function evaluations: • Singular logits. As noise vanishes, token posteriors approach point masses, requiring unbounded logit differences. Our singular logits capture this divergence analytically through a reference posterior, so the network learns only a bounded residual of contextual token preferences. This guarantees that the modeled posterior converges to a one-hot distribution and the trajectory to a token embedding (Section 3.1 ). • Embedding geometry for language flows. Token embeddings define the geometry of corruption and denoising. Our fixed, frequency-weighted Hellinger–SVD embeddings place tokens with similar contexts nearby. Their dimension is a free hyperparameter, which we find important for generation quality (Section 3.2 ). • Logit-space self-conditioning guidance. Self-conditioning guidance extrapolates between predictions with and without the previous clean estimate, which prior work does in continuous state space [ 9 , 27 ] . We instead extrapolate in logit space, so the guided prediction remains a token distribution, learnable through cross-entropy alone with one function evaluation per step (Section 3.3 ). • Regularized reflow. Regularized reflow retrains the model on its own noise–token couplings and interpolates its weights back toward the base model, straightening the flow for few-step generation while controlling drift (Section 3.4 ). 2 Continuous Flow for Discrete Generation Setup.
